sections.b: Ezekiel 16 is the Bible's longest marriage allegory. The LORD finds an abandoned baby girl, raises her, clothes and adorns her, and marries her with an oath. She uses his gifts for idols and sells herself to other nations. Judgment follows, but the chapter ends with an everlasting covenant and atonement. It sits beside Hosea 1–3 and Jeremiah 2–3 and is paired with the story of Oholah and Oholibah in Ezekiel 23. Modern readers disagree on how the image of a shamed wife should be read; the chapter page sets out both sides.

sections.h: Adultery and its penalty in Ezekiel 16
sections.b: Ezekiel 16:38 says the LORD will judge Jerusalem with 'the sentences given to women who commit adultery and shed blood', and 16:40 names stoning, the penalty of the law (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). The marriage in the chapter is a figure for the LORD's covenant with his people, and the chapter gives no rule for human marriage.

Ezekiel 16:3 says Jerusalem's roots are Canaanite: an Amorite father and a Hittite mother. It reflects the Jebusite city David took (2 Samuel 5:6–9). In Ezekiel the city's beauty and fame were the LORD's gift (16:14), and her fall is a loss of what he gave.

Ezekiel 16:49–50 names Sodom's guilt as pride, a full belly, quiet comfort and no help for the poor and needy, then 'something abhorrent'. Jerusalem is said to be worse (16:47–52), and the LORD promises to restore Sodom along with Samaria and Jerusalem (16:53–55). Other texts name other wrongs: abuse of guests (Genesis 19), injustice and lies (Isaiah 1:10; Jeremiah 23:14), inhospitality (Wisdom 19:13–15) and sexual wrong (Jude 7). The readings in Jewish and Christian tradition are set out in the note at 16:49.

In Ezekiel 16:46 Samaria and her daughters (the towns of the northern kingdom) are Jerusalem's older sister, and Sodom the younger. Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and Ezekiel says Samaria did not commit half of Jerusalem's sins (16:51), so Jerusalem sinned more than twice as much. Samaria, Sodom and Jerusalem are all to be restored (16:53–55).

Ezekiel 16:20–21 charges Jerusalem with slaughtering the sons and daughters she bore the LORD and making them 'pass over' to the images. Elsewhere he says children were made to pass 'through the fire' (20:31); 20:26 uses the same verb of the firstborn, without 'fire'. The practice is forbidden in Leviticus 18:21 and is a charge against Ahaz and Manasseh (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6). How widespread it was is debated.
sections.refs: Ezekiel 16:20–21; Ezekiel 20:26; Ezekiel 20:31; Ezekiel 23:37; Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10

sections.b: In Ezekiel 16:15–22 Jerusalem takes the gifts the LORD gave her, the clothes, gold, silver, oil, flour and honey, and uses them to make shrines and male images, and sets his food before them. The prophet calls the idols both 'abhorrent things' and 'filthy idols' (16:36). Chapter 18 repeats idolatry, 'eating on the mountains' and lifting the eyes to 'filthy idols', among the things the righteous person avoids (18:6, 12, 15).

sections.h: High places made of cloth and platforms
sections.b: Ezekiel 16:16 says the bride made 'colorful high places' from her clothes, and 16:24–25, 31, 39 speak of a mound and a high place in every public square and at the head of every road. These are shrines in the open. In 18:6, 11, 15 'eating on the mountains' is the meal at such sites.

sections.h: Marriage, oaths and the everlasting covenant
sections.b: Ezekiel 16:8 calls the LORD's bond with Jerusalem a marriage covenant sworn on oath. In 16:59–63 the broken covenant is answered by 'an everlasting covenant', which the LORD himself sets up and in which he makes atonement. Chapter 17 treats the oath of King Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar as an oath to the LORD, and its breaking as treachery against the LORD's own covenant (17:13–19).
sections.refs: Ezekiel 16:8; Ezekiel 16:59–63; Ezekiel 17:13–19; 2 Chronicles 36:13; Jeremiah 32:40; Ezekiel 37:26

sections.b: Ezekiel 16:63 ends the chapter with the LORD himself as the one who makes atonement, and the forgiven city is left without a word. The verb is kipper, the verb of the Day of Atonement. As in Psalm 65:3 and Psalm 78:38, no sacrifice is named.

Ezekiel 16:26–29 tells Judah's alliances as a woman's affairs with Egypt, Assyria and Chaldea. In 16:34 Jerusalem is the one who pays. Chapter 17 treats Zedekiah's embassy to Egypt for horses and an army as a breach of his oath to Babylon and a doomed hope (17:15–18). Other prophets give the same warning (Isaiah 30:1–7; 31:1; Jeremiah 37:5–10).

sections.h: Egypt as a lover and a broken reed
sections.b: Ezekiel 16:26 calls the Egyptians the neighbors with whom Jerusalem acted as a prostitute; 17:7, 15, 17 make Pharaoh the second great eagle, to whom Zedekiah turned; and 19:3–4 has the first cub led off to Egypt with hooks (Jehoahaz, 609 BC). In all three, Egypt cannot save.

Ezekiel 17:3–4, 12 identify the great eagle that takes the top of the cedar as the king of Babylon, who in 597 BC carried off King Jehoiachin and the leaders (2 Kings 24:12–15). In 19:9 the second cub is brought to the king of Babylon in a cage. Ezekiel treats Babylon as the LORD's instrument and Zedekiah's revolt as a broken oath.

The king of Babylon in Ezekiel 17:12–16 is not named, but he is Nebuchadnezzar. He took Jehoiachin and the leading men to Babylon and set Zedekiah on the throne under a covenant and an oath, intending the kingdom to stay low and loyal (17:13–14). Zedekiah's revolt is said to have been against the LORD's own oath (17:19).

sections.h: Exile in the cedar and the cub
sections.b: Ezekiel 17 pictures the first deportation as an eagle carrying the top of a cedar to a trading city (17:3–4, 12), and chapter 19 pictures two royal cubs taken away, one to Egypt and one to Babylon (19:4, 9). The vine of 19:13 is planted in a dry desert. Chapter 18 is the exiles' chapter: it tells them the door of repentance is open.
sections.refs: Ezekiel 17:3–4; Ezekiel 17:12; Ezekiel 19:4; Ezekiel 19:9; Ezekiel 19:13; Ezekiel 18:30–32

sections.h: The low vine and the burned vine
sections.b: Ezekiel 17:5–10 uses a low, spreading vine for a kingdom that was meant to stay small and loyal; 19:10–14 uses a fruitful vine with strong branches for the royal line, torn up and burned. In chapter 15 the vine is worthless wood. All three are set beside the vine songs of Isaiah 5:1–7 and Psalm 80.

The LORD says he will take a tender shoot from the top of the cedar and plant it on Israel's high mountain. The Targum reads it of a king from David's line, Rashi of the King Messiah, and Radak of Zerubbabel. Christian readers take it as Christ. It is one of several shoot or branch promises (Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 6:12), and the birds nesting in its shade are echoed in Mark 4:30–32.

sections.h: A new shoot from the cedar
sections.b: After the royal line is cut off (chapters 17 and 19), the LORD promises in Ezekiel 17:22–24 to plant a tender shoot taken from the top of the cedar. It is one of the passages in which the promise to David (2 Samuel 7) is carried through the exile; the leaders' lament in chapter 19 mourns the same line.

Ezekiel calls Judah's rulers 'leaders' (nesi'im) in 19:1 and pictures them as lion cubs of the lioness of Judah (19:2–9; compare Genesis 49:9). Two are taken in hooks and a cage: the first to Egypt, the second to Babylon. The poem lists no crime but mourns the end of the line.

Ezekiel is told to sing laments for the leaders of Israel (19:1), the city of Tyre (26:17; 27:2), the king of Tyre (28:12) and Pharaoh (32:2). Chapter 19 is a lament for kings who are not yet all dead; its last line says it is a lament and has become one.

Ezekiel is told to speak a riddle and a parable (17:2) about two eagles and a vine, and the LORD explains it (17:11–21). Chapter 16 has a mashal in the proverb 'Like mother, like daughter' (16:44), and chapter 18 a proverb the LORD forbids (18:2–3).

Ezekiel 18 is the Bible's longest argument about whether children pay for their parents' sins. The exiles quote a proverb that they do; the LORD forbids it and says the person who sins is the one who will die. The chapter sets this beside Exodus 20:5 and 34:7, Deuteronomy 24:16 and Jeremiah 31:29–30 (see individual responsibility). It also records the people's charge that the Lord's way is not fair and the LORD's reply (18:25, 29).
sections.refs: Ezekiel 18:2–4; Ezekiel 18:20; Ezekiel 18:25; Exodus 20:5; Deuteronomy 24:16; Jeremiah 31:29–30

sections.h: The person who sins will die
sections.b: Ezekiel 18:4 and 18:20 say the person (nefesh) who sins is the one who will die. The Hebrew nefesh is a life or a person; the verse is a rule of justice and is not a teaching about the nature of the soul, although some groups cite it for that. Chapter 18 sets out righteous and wicked deeds in lists (18:5–9, 10–13, 14–17) and shows that either can turn.

Ezekiel 18:20, 'a son will not bear the guilt of his father', is sometimes brought into the debate over original sin. The card on the chapter page sets out what Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Methodist and Baptist texts say about Adam's sin. The texts quoted there do not themselves cite Ezekiel 18, and the note at 18:20 asks what that verse is about: a court and a person's own blame.

Ezekiel 18:21–32 is the Bible's fullest statement that repentance changes a person's standing before God. A wicked person who turns away from sin will live; a righteous person who turns to wrong will die. The one verb shuv carries both 'turn back' and 'turn away from'. The chapter ends: 'turn back and live'.

Ezekiel 18:31 commands the people to make themselves a new heart and a new spirit. In Ezekiel 36:26 the LORD says he will give them one. Augustine prayed 'Give what you command' and used such verses against Pelagius; Reformed and Wesleyan readers take the command differently (see the note at 18:31).

sections.h: Does God want the death of the wicked?
sections.b: Ezekiel 18:23 and 18:32 say God takes no pleasure in anyone's death. The verses are cited in discussions of predestination and election, with 1 Timothy 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9. The chapter page shows how Reformed, Lutheran, Methodist, Catholic and Baptist teachings use them.

Ezekiel 18:24 and 18:26 say a righteous person who turns to injustice will die, and his earlier righteous acts will not be remembered. Churches differ on how this fits the assurance of final salvation: Reformed and Baptist teaching on perseverance, Catholic teaching on mortal sin, Orthodox teaching on grace and co-operation, and Methodist teaching on falling from grace.

Ezekiel 18:8, 13 and 17 list lending at interest and taking a profit among the sins of the wicked, and refusing them among the deeds of the righteous. It follows the law against charging an Israelite interest (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36–37; Deuteronomy 23:19). Ezekiel also lists it among Jerusalem's crimes in 22:12.

sections.h: The righteous person and the poor
sections.b: The righteous person in Ezekiel 18 feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, returns a pledge and does not oppress the poor and needy (18:7, 16, 17); the sin of Sodom in 16:49 is the opposite: she did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.

Ezekiel 18:6 includes in the just man's deeds that he does not go near a woman during her monthly uncleanness. The rule is that of Leviticus 18:19 and 20:18; Ezekiel lists its breaking among the crimes of Jerusalem in 22:10.

sections.h: Ezekiel 18 and the sour grapes proverb
sections.b: Ezekiel 18 is the central text for this subject. It quotes the exiles' proverb (18:2), forbids it, and states the rule that the person who sins will die and that a son does not bear his father's guilt (18:4, 20). It is read with Jeremiah 31:29–30, Deuteronomy 24:16 and 2 Kings 14:6, and set beside Exodus 20:5 and 34:7. See the chapter page for how Jewish and Christian readers fit them together.
